articles.title: Meet Bailey Quinn Frank, 15, from Fort Lauderdale, who built an air sampler with a small fan and filter paper to collect bacterial DNA; she has now won a $25,000 science prize among nearly 2,000 applicants
articles.summary: A 15-year-old student from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, has won a $25,000 science award for developing an affordable device that collects airborne bacterial
articles.body: A 15-year-old student from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, has won a $25,000 science award for developing an affordable device that collects airborne bacterial DNA, with the potential to help communities monitor environmental health risks. Bailey Quinn Frank received the top prize at the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge, announced on October 27. According to the official announcement by Society for Science, Bailey designed a low-cost environmental DNA sampler using a small fan and filter paper to collect airborne bacteria. She was selected as the winner from a group of 30 finalists chosen from nearly 2,000 applicants across 47 states and five US territories.How Bailey developed an affordable air samplerBailey’s project focused on environmental DNA, commonly known as eDNA, which allows researchers to study genetic material collected from the environment and identify organisms present in a particular location. She explored whether an inexpensive device could capture airborne genetic material and support the detection of bacterial pathogens.According to her finalist profile published by Society for Science, Bailey built her sampler by attaching filter paper to small fans. When switched on, the fans drew air through the device, allowing environmental material, including bacterial DNA, to collect on the paper. She collected two indoor air samples and one outdoor sample. After collecting the material, she purified DNA from the filter papers and transferred part of the collected sample to petri dishes to grow the bacteria. She recorded the bacterial colonies after one week and attempted to identify them.Bailey also sent her best samples for 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing, a technique commonly used to help identify and classify bacteria. Her project examined whether the device could provide useful information about the microorganisms present in different environments.What her research revealed about indoor and outdoor airBailey’s preliminary findings showed differences between the bacterial communities in indoor and outdoor air samples. The indoor samples contained more bacterial genera associated with people, while the outdoor sample included bacteria associated with soil, water, air and plants. These findings helped demonstrate how an inexpensive sampler could collect material for further investigation of the microorganisms present in an environment. The work also showed how students can apply scientific methods to questions involving public health and environmental monitoring.The device was designed around readily available materials rather than specialised, expensive equipment. This approach is important because the cost of collecting and analysing environmental samples can be a barrier for communities and institutions with limited resources. However, the project represents an early investigation rather than a validated disease-monitoring system. More testing would be needed to establish how reliably the sampler detects specific pathogens, how its performance compares with established equipment and whether it can support routine health surveillance.Why the device could matter for rural communitiesBailey was particularly interested in the challenges faced by rural communities, where access to resources for disease surveillance may be limited. Monitoring environmental samples could potentially help researchers identify microorganisms in an area and investigate possible health risks. Her idea was to explore whether a simple, low-cost sampler could make environmental DNA collection more accessible. If further research establishes its reliability, such a device could offer a practical starting point for collecting samples in locations where sophisticated monitoring equipment is difficult to obtain.Bailey’s interest in the subject was also shaped by her personal experience with coeliac disease, according to her Society for Science profile. She said that the experience helped her develop empathy for other children and adults whose health conditions make them feel different from their peers. Outside research, she enjoys making art, including digital art, watercolour, fabric and clay projects. She is also involved in the Technology Student Association, where she has developed technical and leadership skills through activities related to medical technology, community service and career preparation.$25,000 award recognises research and teamworkBailey received the $25,000 Thermo Fisher Scientific ASCEND Award, the highest prize at the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. The award recognised her environmental DNA project as well as her performance in the competition’s team challenges. The competition brought together 30 finalists selected from nearly 2,000 applicants representing 47 states and five territories. The finalists collectively received more than $100,000 in awards, while each finalist’s school received a $1,000 grant to support science, technology, engineering and mathematics education.Alongside evaluating individual research projects, the competition tested participants’ critical thinking, creativity, communication and collaboration. Challenges included designing sustainable cities, prioritising patients during a simulated outbreak, exploring the use of artificial intelligence to identify turtle species and building protective enclosures for diamondback terrapin eggs. Other leading award recipients included Henry Grover and his twin brother Jack Grover, who investigated whether a water-absorbing gel could help prevent wildfires from reigniting. Myreen Ahsan used machine learning to identify molecules that could potentially target a protein associated with frontotemporal dementia, while Wileidy Enid Feliciano-Rivera developed biodegradable mulch from plantain peels.Bailey’s award highlights how an accessible scientific question can lead to a project combining practical engineering with environmental research. Although her sampler requires further evaluation before it can be used for routine health surveillance, her work demonstrates the potential of young researchers to explore affordable approaches to real-world challenges.

articles.title: Do spiders dream? Researchers studying Australian jumping spiders have found sleep patterns resembling REM sleep, raising new questions about dream-like states in invertebrates
articles.summary: Dreaming is an experience we often associate with humans but is it something that only humans experience?
articles.body: Dreaming is an experience we often associate with humans but is it something that only humans experience? Scientists have long been curious to ascertain what may happen when other animals fall asleep. While certain sleep behaviours have been observed in mammals and birds, much less is known about how sleep works in creatures with a distinct nervous system. Researchers at the University of Bonn have studied the Australian jumping spider, Portia fimbriata, known to be a clever hunter. As Science Daily reported on the 27th of October 2026, researchers have discovered evidence of distinct sleep stages, including one that resembles the rapid eye movement (REM) sleep seen in humans, opening up new questions about whether spiders could experience something resembling dreams.The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Bonn in Germany, examined the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata. The findings, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, by monitoring the spiders on several days and nights found clear evidence that spiders experience regulated sleep, and a REM-like sleep that is “marked by eye movements and muscle twitches” .The observations also suggest that some features of sleep may be shared by animals separated by considerable evolutionary differences.A research study: Portia fimbriata The choice of spider is particularly interesting because Portia fimbriata is known for its sophisticated hunting behaviour. Members of the genus Portia prey on other spiders and use different strategies to approach and capture them which include imitating the vibrations of insects struggling in a webb, that can draw another spider towards what appears to be potential prey.Such behaviour has made these spiders interesting subjects for researchers investigating animal learning and cognition. Their hunting strategies also raise questions about how their nervous systems support complex behaviour, making their sleep patterns another avenue for scientific investigation. Although scientists have previously reported REM-like movements in jumping spiders, establishing whether these movements occur during genuine sleep required further investigation. The latest study set out to examine not only the movements themselves but also whether the spiders showed other behavioural signs associated with sleep.What happens when spiders fall asleep?To observe the spiders, the researchers recorded their behaviour over several days and nights, using infrared cameras to monitor them in darkness. Each individual Portia fimbriata spider was placed in the plastic dishes measuring 12 centimeters in diameter. The animal was also monitored in different lighting conditions to examine distinguishable sleeping stages. The infrared camera helped monitor and reveal their distinct sleeping stages, The recordings revealed two distinguishable sleep stages, including a period of quiet rest followed by a stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches, however this response does not necessarily mean that these animals experience the same REM sleep like humans.These movements are particularly noteworthy because rapid eye movements and changes in muscle activity are associated with REM sleep in humans and other vertebrates. The similarities prompted researchers to investigate whether the spiders' behaviour represented a distinct stage of sleep rather than ordinary inactivity.However, the resemblance does not establish that spiders dream. The researchers relied on behavioural observations rather than direct examination of their brain activity, meaning they could not determine whether the spiders experienced dreams or what might occur in their brains during these periods.The team also tested how readily the spiders responded to sound to test whether they were asleep or just lay motionless. During the observed sleep stages, their responses to disturbances were delayed compared with when they were awake, and some spiders did not respond at all. Researchers additionally investigated "sleep rebound", a phenomenon in which an animal makes up for disrupted sleep afterwards. Together, these observations provided evidence that the spiders experience regulated sleep with distinct stages, strengthening the case that their nighttime behaviour involves more than simply resting.Can spiders dream then? Sciene Daily has come to note that while the Bonn University is in the process of expanding its research, what remains to be explored is the relationship between sleep and cognitive abilties. However, what the research does tell us is that creatures that are seemingly small and jumpy can have complex sleeping systems just like us humans.Whether spiders can dream or not still remains to be know, but the ongoing inquiry and isnghts into the spiders night time behavouir and responses to external factors has offered a way for understandign how widley different features are distributed across the animal kingdom, with the research time likely to expand the inquiry into how animals sleep in their natural environments.

articles.title: Here’s Virgin Galactic’s new Apeiron spaceship
articles.summary: Virgin Galactic unveiled its new Apeiron spacecraft, which is now expected to launch in Q2 2027.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic’s new spaceship is here, dubbed “Apeiron” by popular vote from a public poll. Apeiron is the first of the company’s new Delta-class spacecraft, but it isn’t slated to launch for nearly another year. Earlier this week, Virgin Galactic announced another delay in its launch timeline: > The lead Spaceship’s first commercial spaceflight is now expected in early Q2 2027, and the second Spaceship is expected to begin commercial spaceflight operations in late Q2/early Q3 2027. The updated timeline reflects additional time for completing avionics software integration and validation, which uses an exhaustive testing process. That testing will conclude at Spaceport America as the lead Spaceship is readied for its flight test series. [Media: Virgin Galactic had previously delayed its next commercial spaceflight to February 2027, rather than late 2026. It’s now been over two years since Virgin Galactic’s last commercial spaceflight in June 2024, when it retired its VSS Unity spacecraft. Apeiron is leaving Virgin Galactic’s Mesa, Arizona Spaceship Factory on Wednesday onboard a captive-carry flight with its Eve launch vehicle, heading to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where Virgin Galactic says its “engineering team plans to complete avionics software validation before beginning flight tests.”

articles.title: A Minnesota farmer harvesting corn found a mysterious 11-foot-wide metallic object in his field; space experts now suspect it is debris from a Chinese rocket launched in September, but its origin remains unconfirmed
articles.summary: On the afternoon of 14 October, a farmer in Scott Township, Stevens County, western Minnesota, was walking through his cornfield when he stumbled upon
articles.body: On the afternoon of 14 October, a farmer in Scott Township, Stevens County, western Minnesota, was walking through his cornfield when he stumbled upon something that did not belong there. The metal was charred and round, about 11 feet across. He couldn’t say what it was, so he dialled the sheriff’s office. The deputies who went out to look agreed: it was unusual. It looked like the premise of Steven Spielberg’s latest UFO blockbuster flick. All they knew was that it was not farm equipment.What is the mysterious object?In a press release from the sheriff’s office, officials described it as “a large metallic object”. They said the object was “presumably a space object”. State and federal agencies were called in to investigate the debris and help remove it from the property. “Agency officials have determined that there is no danger to the public due to this incident,” the sheriff’s office assured the public. But the pressing questions remained: what was the object, and where did it come from?The object may have lain in the field for about six weeks, through the growing season and into harvest, local outlets, including the Rapid City Post and NBC affiliates KARE 11 and 9News, reported. Either way, no one knew it was there until the farmer found it. Scott Township is home to about 117 people, which helps explain how something of this size could go unnoticed.This information has led some experts to suspect that the debris may have come from a rocket. The metal matches the upper stage of a Zhuque-2E, a rocket built by the Chinese company LandSpace. It lifted off on 15 September from north-western China with 10 satellites for the Qianfan network, a project intended to rival SpaceX’s Starlink. That same night, people in Kansas, Minnesota and Wisconsin filmed fireballs crossing the sky. Ars Technica has linked those videos to the rocket.The measurements are the strongest clue. The upper stage is about 3.35 metres across, close to the 11 feet reported in the field. Some reports suggest that the metal could be the end cap of a fuel tank. That is a useful description, but it is not yet a confirmed identification.Under the 1972 Space Liability Convention, the country that launches a space object is liable for any damage it causes on Earth.This incident is not the first of its kind. Over the years, similar debris has turned up in other places. In July, metal spheres washed ashore in Australia and were traced to a launch vehicle. In Indonesia, a large metal object found in a palm oil plantation is also being investigated as a possible Zhuque-2E fragment. Reports say the same rocket’s upper stage broke apart in orbit during an earlier flight in June.Meanwhile, official confirmation of the identity of this unusual metallic object found on a Minnesota farm is still pending. The sheriff’s office says investigators are working to determine the object’s origin.

articles.title: New tool intends to help python hunters. How much can they make?
articles.summary: A tool created by University of Florida researchers aims to guide Burmese python removal efforts by helping hunters prioritize snakes for capture.
articles.body:
A tool created by University of Florida researchers aims to guide Burmese python removal efforts by helping hunters prioritize snakes for capture .

Researchers associated with the University of Florida and the South Florida Water Management District developed and tested a weighted removal index (WRI), according to the study, published in Ecological Applications on Sept. 21 . The index estimates the effect of removing individual pythons on the potential growth of the population.

"What we want to optimize for is not just how many pythons do we take out of the ecosystem, but how can we most impact the stability, the growth, the persistence of these populations?" said Alexander Romer, quantitative ecologist at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences and lead author of the study.

The weighted index takes survival and reproductive potential into consideration. Removing mature female pythons, for instance, could more greatly affect future population growth than removing hatchlings.

"We know that the juveniles, they have a lot higher mortality than the adults," Romer said. "And those adults, especially in Florida, have really low predation rates. There's a couple things that will eat them, but mostly it's humans that are especially removing the full-grown animals. We count all of the removals equally, but are all of the removals actually having an equal impact?"

Ultimately, part of the goal is for python hunters to benefit from the WRI. Since Burmese pythons are so "cryptic," the study states that removal programs "benefit" from tools that support decision-making and "prioritize effort toward high-impact removals, rather than treating all captures as equivalent."

"The most impactful factor on whether removal occurs or not is the person running the survey," Romer said. "That tells you that we can try to look into these variables, but ultimately the experience and knowledge and skill of these contractors is extremely important to making this program run."

Contractors could use a "demographic weighting scheme" for Burmese pythons to target "key demographics," which could make efforts to manage the python population more efficient and reduce the resources required for removal, according to the paper.

"Models of invasive species control" suggest that removing members of the population based on demographics can help speed up population suppression, says the study, which cited research showing that removing "large reproductive females" had the biggest impact on the population vital rates of Brown treesnakes.

"A lot of these contractors have a really impressive knowledge of the Everglades, of python biology, and because they're putting that knowledge into practice, it actually makes this management system work," Romer said. "Contractors do a very good job at solving a very hard problem, and we're trying to help them accomplish that."

Mature snakes removed during winter months

Total python removals were highest from June through August, according to the study, mostly due to the high number of "hatchlings" during the summer.

In winter, though there were fewer overall captures, the pythons that were removed were more likely to be mature adults. Winter months "contributed a disproportionate share of total" weighted removal index, "despite having far fewer captures," which reflected the removal of "large, demographically important" adult snakes.

Removing snakes during the "breeding season" also causes "disproportionate demographic impacts," according to the study.

Florida's professional Burmese python hunters

Two initiatives, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission's Python Action Team Removing Invasive Constrictors (PATRIC) program and the South Florida Water Management District's python elimination program , work "in tandem" to compensate qualified people with "nonnative constrictor control experience," according to the FWC's website.

Being a state contractor is "demanding," according to the PATRIC application form, which says that "most contractors" remove "over 30 pythons per year."

"As of April 2025, over 23,500 pythons have been removed from natural areas in the state of Florida," reads the FWC's website. "Of that total, over 11,000 pythons have been removed by FWC PATRIC and SFWMD PEP contractors since program inception."

The department says that "hunters, anglers" and other "outdoor recreationists with experience removing pythons or other large constrictors from the wild" should apply.

How much can Burmese python hunters make?

The South Florida Water Management District's python elimination program contracts python "removal agents" to work "on designated lands across South Florida, including in Monroe, Miami-Dade, Broward, Collier, Hendry, Lee, and Palm Beach counties," according to its website.

The program pays contractors a variable hourly survey rate , which depends on the area they're searching, according to the program's FAQ. Regular pay is $14 per hour , premium pay is $20 per hour and ultra-premium pay is $30 per hour, with 10 billable hours per day.

An additional incentive is paid "for every python removed based on length," according to the program's website — $50 for the first four feet and $25 per foot for every foot after four.

Additionally, $200 will be paid for any verified active python nest, and $50 for the "documented catch and release of any telemetered research pythons."

Burmese pythons pose a threat to Florida's native species

Adult Burmese pythons have few predators, according to the FWC , and frequently prey upon native species, including those that are threatened or endangered .

Burmese pythons can also threaten the safety of human beings, although they ultimately pose the biggest danger to the ecosystems they become established in. They can also prey on household pets, such as cats and dogs.

Though Burmese pythons can grow to over 20 feet in length, those captured in Florida are usually between six and 10 feet long, says the FWC . In adulthood, they're larger than almost all native snakes, and are usually tan with dark blotches along their backs and sides.

Additionally, the dark patches along their bodies usually fit together like puzzle pieces, and can look similar to the patterns on giraffes. They also have dark wedges along the tops and bottoms of their heads, as well as behind their eyes.

Sarah Perkel is a South Florida Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network's Florida Connect team. You can get all of Florida's best content directly in your inbox each weekday day by signing up for the free newsletter, Florida TODAY .

articles.title: Trump DOE loans $5B to nuclear plants that will power data centers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Constellation Energy will get $5 billion in government loans to modernize nuclear reactors. Most of the new capacity is already committed to Google, Amazon, and Meta.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is giving Constellation Energy $5 billion in loans to expand nuclear generating capacity at eight power plants by 1.1 gigawatts.

Most or all of the additional power from seven of those facilities has already been bought by Google, Meta, or Amazon.

Constellation said it plans to use the financing to “uprate” 11 existing reactors, an industry term for expanding capacity at a reactor, often by using more highly enriched uranium and by upgrading equipment to handle the increased power levels.

The energy company said it had already committed to spending more than $7 billion to add 1,080 megawatts of nuclear capacity to deliver power to Google, Amazon, and Meta. The loan commitment, which has yet to be finalized, “could lower financing costs” for the projects, Constellation said in a press release .

The eight power plants include six in Illinois (Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle, and Quad Cities), one in Maryland (Calvert Cliffs), and one in Pennsylvania (Limerick).

Google is already the confirmed buyer of additional power from the Pennsylvania plant and four Illinois power plants, while Amazon is buying electricity from the Maryland plant and Meta is effectively buying the entire Clinton power plant in Illinois.

On Tuesday, the Department of Energy touted the loan as supporting “affordable, reliable power to American homes and businesses,” though there is no evidence that the new nuclear capacity will lower prices for residential ratepayers. Constellation’s announcement does not say whether the projects will maintain or lower electricity rates, and the company would not confirm the government’s claim to TechCrunch.

Hyperscalers, including Google, Amazon, and Meta, have been scouring the grid for additional capacity to support their AI data centers. Tech companies are paying handsomely for energy, committing tens of billions of dollars over the coming years. Given that power has become a competitive advantage, that estimate is probably on the low end.

By lowering the cost of capital for the upgrades, the Department of Energy’s loans could boost Constellation’s bottom line, that of the hyperscalers — or both.

articles.title: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind and a surprising new find in a well-studied group
articles.summary: Hidden among the roots of trees in China’s lush forests, an extraordinary organism has emerged as a reminder that nature still has plenty of surprises in
articles.body: Hidden among the roots of trees in China’s lush forests, an extraordinary organism has emerged as a reminder that nature still has plenty of surprises in store. Rising nearly 20 inches above the forest floor and weighing close to five pounds, the newly identified fungus is challenging scientists’ understanding of how large certain fungal structures can become. Its remarkable dimensions are not its only distinction: genetic evidence suggests its evolutionary lineage dates back approximately 65 million years. Scroll down to read the details.Meet D-rex, the fungal giantNamed Dianjunus rex and nicknamed D-rex, the species was discovered during surveys of forest environments in Yunnan province, southwestern China. According to ScienceDaily, researchers from the Kunming Institute of Botany encountered unusual whitish structures growing from the woody roots of Chinese cork oak trees.These structures, known as stromata, are reproductive formations that produce spores. Reaching approximately 50 centimetres in height and weighing up to 2.2 kilograms, they are the largest known fruiting bodies among fungi belonging to the phylum Ascomycota.As reported by People, previously known fruiting bodies in this group generally reached considerably smaller heights, making D-rex an exceptional discovery even within a major fungal group comprising tens of thousands of recognised species.A new branch on the fungal family treeThe scientists initially suspected they had encountered an unfamiliar fungus. However, laboratory investigations revealed something more significant. By examining its physical characteristics, cultivating its spores and analysing its DNA, the team established that the organism was sufficiently distinct to warrant an entirely new genus and family, Dianjunaceae.ScienceDaily reports that D-rex belongs to the order Xylariales, a group known for producing specialised compounds and enzymes that help break down complex plant material. Researchers believe the newly identified fungus may similarly obtain nutrients by decomposing dead wood, although its precise ecological role requires further investigation.An evolutionary link to the age of dinosaursPerhaps the most intriguing aspect of the discovery lies in its ancient origins. Using molecular-clock analysis, researchers compared the fungus’s genetic information with that of hundreds of other fungal species to estimate when its lineage first emerged.The findings suggest that Dianjunaceae originated around 65 million years ago, approximately one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction that wiped out non-avian dinosaurs.According to People, this timeline has prompted researchers to consider whether the environmental upheaval following the extinction created new opportunities for wood-decomposing fungi. Changes in forest ecosystems and the availability of dead plant material may have helped ancestral fungi diversify.Why does it grow so large?According to ScienceDaily, scientists are still investigating what enabled D-rex to develop such towering reproductive structures. One possibility is that its height improves spore dispersal, allowing spores to catch air currents above vegetation and debris on the forest floor.However, producing such a large structure requires considerable energy. Its unusual size may therefore represent an evolutionary advantage in particular forest conditions rather than a strategy that would benefit every fungus.More discoveries could be waitingThe finding also highlights the remarkable biodiversity of East Asian forests, where varied habitats and complex ecological relationships support unusual organisms. As ScienceDaily notes, difficult terrain, seasonal growth patterns and the often-hidden nature of fungi have made many species challenging to document.Further exploration may reveal more unexpected fungal forms, offering scientists fresh insights into evolution, forest ecosystems and the extraordinary diversity of life that remains undiscovered.Image Courtesy: Kunming Institute of Botany / Chinese Academy of Sciences

articles.title: You can see every red flag in Theranos 2.0
articles.summary: Following You Can See Everything, there are some concerning signs that Haemanthus, aka Theranos 2.0, is following the same playbook.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. From afar, it’s easy to look back at the Theranos debacle and scream at Nathan Fielder that, obviously, Elizabeth Holmes is lying in You Can See Everything. In the weeks since the movie’s release, journalists and whistleblowers alike have rushed to remind moviegoers of Holmes’ numerous documented lies. Chief among the facts: The Theranos device never worked as advertised. But Fielder’s aim with this film wasn’t relitigating Theranos. Even the most mind-bending of three-hour documentaries doesn’t have enough time to fully tackle the quagmire that was the secretive biotech startup. It’s worth remembering that Theranos was a prime example of overinflating what technology can do. It sure would be nice if a single droplet of blood could be run in a magical machine and beep boop — you’ve got accurate results for over a hundred diagnostic tests. It’s a compelling concept, but the existing science doesn’t support the idea. As I wrote in last week’s Optimizer, you simply can’t test for every disease from blood alone. Sometimes, a blood test is merely part of a multistep process to rule out what you don’t have. A finger prick carries a higher risk of rupturing blood cells, which can skew test results. Your finger is more prone to surface contamination because hands are dirty by nature. Compared to drawing blood from a vein, a finger prick may not be purely blood — it often mixes with interstitial fluid, diluting the sample. Different biomarkers can require wholly different testing procedures, making the small volume collected difficult to work with. These are just some of the practical challenges Theranos had to solve to be better than the clinical gold standard. It couldn’t, and that’s why they had to fake it by bringing in Siemens devices that used traditional blood testing methods. That makes it even more astonishing that Holmes and her partner Billy Evans spend a chunk of the film actively working on what Evans casually calls Theranos 2.0. This new venture, Haemanthus, involves a similar diagnostic device that uses… lasers. The official line is that Holmes is not helming the effort, but Evans refers to it as “getting the band back together.” The film purposefully blurs the lines between truth and lies. But with nascent health tech, it’s genuinely hard for the average person to distinguish promising medical advancements from snake oil. If you left You Can See Everything wondering if there’s any truth to using lasers to diagnose conditions — you don’t have to watch microbiology videos at twice the speed to find out. Instead, here are a few extra tips when it comes to spotting shenanigans straight out of the wellness grifter playbook. Technology is not magic In the documentary, Fielder likens Holmes to a magician. Technology, no matter how powerful or well crafted, is never magic. But going along with Fielder’s metaphor, magicians succeed through misdirection. Evans presents lasers in the film as though they’re a little-known marvel — a key technology Theranos was missing — and that Haemanthus will be the first to make them truly useful. Based on a patent published by The New York Times, Haemanthus uses Raman spectroscopy. For the record, Raman spectroscopy does involve lasers, but it’s not a new technology. It was first discovered in 1928. In a nutshell, this laser tech is used to identify chemical structures in a molecule. There are myriad biological and medical uses for it, including noninvasively studying tissue samples. But will it, as a New York Times report describes, “identify and qualify biomarkers such as glucose and hormones” and then use AI to “detect cancer and infections”? [Image: With Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes often spoke of technology like it was some magical force that would usher in a new era. Researchers are exploring using this tech to diagnose early-stage cancers. They’re also looking into using it for glucose monitoring. Does that mean this is a better method than what currently exists? Maybe for certain cases, but probably not in every scenario. In medicine, it’s common to require multiple tests for diagnosis. Similarly, there are often multiple ways to treat the same condition. It’s often a game of weighing pros and cons for various approaches. There are too many unknown factors to accurately comment on Haemanthus, but it’s concerning that Evans zeroes in on lasers like they’re a panacea for everything that plagued Theranos. When investors, journalists, and the public ask hard questions, founders love to sprinkle technology into their rhetoric like it’s fairy dust. You can see it happening right now with AI. But tech is a tool. Any tool will have pros and cons, situations it excels in and scenarios it’s ill suited for. It’s not always a grift, but anytime an executive shows signs of magical thinking or inflates what technology can do, your bullshit alarm should be ringing. Tech likes to move fast, medicine really doesn’t In recent history, I can think of exactly one time the public health sector truly hauled ass to make something happen: the covid-19 vaccine. The vaccine took roughly 10 months to develop, compared to the typical five-to-15-year timeline. But even then, it was a Herculean effort requiring global coordination and tens of billions of dollars, largely from the government. (That’s not including the billions invested in researching mRNA vaccines during the three decades prior to the pandemic.) It was a heartening feat of human ingenuity — but again, it took 10 months built on 30 years of foundational research and several billion dollars. So it’s an immediate red flag when Evans says in the documentary that Haemanthus would have a novel, revolutionary prototype working in about a year. Case in point, he said that in 2023, and it’s already 2026. But even if lasers were the key to everything, there’s no way in hell something like this would breeze through the regulatory process. Not much is known about Haemanthus. It has no website, unless you count a sparse LinkedIn page that says the company has two to 10 employees and is working on “AI-native sensors for health,” a technology that “captures thousands of biomarkers.” The bulk of what’s publicly known comes from You Can See Everything and a 2025 New York Times article, which states Haemanthus is building a device that uses a “laser to scan blood, saliva, or urine from pets and analyze the sample on a molecular level.” (The startup is apparently aiming to do veterinary tests first before perhaps eventually graduating to humans.) Its “long-term goal” is a “stamp-size, wearable version” of its product for humans, which will “require three years and $70 million.” [Image: Researchers are already using Raman spectroscopy. In this photo, it’s being used to identify dosage and chemical makeup in a sample. This is an incredibly expeditious timeline for any medical device, let alone a novel one. Not least because the biggest names in wearable technology right now can only detect — not diagnose — signs of perhaps two or three conditions. The holy grail is considered noninvasive continuous glucose monitoring, an endeavor that started in 1975 and that Apple has been rumored to be working on for over 15 years now. In 2023, I did a deep dive into why you shouldn’t expect this to arrive on smartwatches anytime soon. The reasons ranged from weak signals and regulatory mazes to skin color impacting how light reflects and battery life. In 2026, not much has changed on this front. Meanwhile, take the continuous glucose monitor. Attempts to monitor glucose levels started in the mid-1800s, but a portable way to monitor glucose didn’t emerge until the 1960s. The first FDA-approved CGM was the Medtronic MiniMed in 1999, but it could only be worn for three days, and data couldn’t be viewed live. A clinician had to review it and inform the patient afterward. The first real-time CGM wasn’t available until 2004, the first over-the-counter CGMs didn’t hit the market until 2024, and only this year did Abbott announce a CGM that can measure two biomarkers. AI advancements could theoretically help remove some technological roadblocks that may, in turn, speed up the overall process. But you know what AI doesn’t really replace? The absolutely labyrinthine regulatory approval and clearance process. You can have a product made and ready to go, only to have it held up in regulatory limbo for years. It’s happened to several Withings products. The infamous wearable taint zapper took six years, an untold number of testing bunnies, and at least a million dollars to hit the market. It’s why wearable companies are currently lobbying in Washington, likely spending mountains of cash to lower these hurdles. So the next time a biotech startup promises something revolutionary relatively fast, it’s usually a pretty good sign they’re either delusional or not telling you the whole truth. Beware anyone who doesn’t show their work Another red flag with Theranos was that the company never published its research or submitted it for peer review. Haemanthus’ pseudo-secrecy — if you really wanted to build in stealth, why would you talk about it at length in a documentary? — is another concerning sign. Perhaps because of Theranos, health tech companies have begun publishing more of their science. Oura, Apple, and Google are all great examples of companies that have published clinical and peer-reviewed research in reputable journals, as well as white papers explaining their features. The act of publishing doesn’t get you a hall pass from scrutiny. Science-washing in the wellness and health sectors is rampant, with some companies using consumer perception studies as “evidence” instead of more rigorous studies. Or, if clinical studies are done, they’re often more of a vanity project than a groundbreaking revelation. Lastly, not all peer-reviewed papers are created equal. You have to be able to read and analyze the fine print to tell if the study itself was done well. However, the absence of any reviewable research should sound the alarm for anyone who values science. In early 2015, months before the damning Wall Street Journal report, Stanford University professor John P.A. Ioannidis penned a critique of Theranos’ lack of peer-reviewed research in JAMA. Theranos responded by siccing its lawyers on Ioannidis in an attempt to get him to retract his opinion. That’s sketchy as hell — especially for any biotech or health tech company. Based on these criteria, Theranos and Haemanthus set off a cacophony of obvious warning bells. But they’re not the only ones. Every year at CES, there are plenty of health tech startups peddling dubious concepts and vaporware right next to people genuinely doing the work. Health is the most valuable thing anyone has, so it’s not always easy to see false promises when your eyes are clouded by hope. No one wants to be sick, and technological miracles are an easier pill to swallow than the protracted ups and downs of real science. But if there’s one thing I took away from You Can See Everything, it’s that Theranos’ playbook is still, unfortunately, alive and well.

articles.title: Elon Musk a 'real genius', Putin says after talks with SpaceX boss
articles.summary: The Russian President praised Musk and said they are in "close" contact.
articles.body:
Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.

The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.

"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."

Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.

Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".

"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.

Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.

The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".

"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.

Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.

US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.

Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.

Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".

Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.

The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of the biggest political allies and financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.

articles.title: Dubai is growing coral in hotel lagoons before moving it back to the sea; the unusual nursery has produced more than 2,500 coral fragments
articles.summary: Dubai is typically famous for its real estate restoration.
articles.body: Dubai is typically famous for its real estate restoration. It is a success story of turning a desert landscape into a world class city today with high rises all around. The architectural wonders, from the Burj Khalifa to incredible builds, attract the attention of anyone visiting the city. However, the oil-exporting city has taken up a fresh initiative to embrace the natural elements surrounding the city. The renowned Jumeirah Hotel started a pilot project for conservation of coral reefs. Today, the initiative comes under the Dubai Reef which is one of Gulf’s most ambitious coral conservation projects. It is led by the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism (DET) which aims to restore biodiversity across Dubai’s sea line.Why Coral Reefs MatterCorals are mesmerising structures of tiny marine animals to create some of the ocean’s most extraordinary wonders. They are often called “rainforests of the sea” as they provide shelter, food and breeding grounds for other marine species. Beneath the waves, they form a vibrant world where life flourishes in a kaleidoscope of colours, shapes and movement. Yet, these underwater treasures are far more than a feast for the eyes. Coral reefs act as natural barriers, protecting coastlines from powerful waves and storms.The coral ecosystems are one of the most sensitive to exist, with requirements of specific temperatures and salinity levels. Any fluctuation in these parameters can lead to death of entire colonies of corals. Today, rising ocean temperatures, coral bleaching, pollution and ocean acidification threaten their delicate existence. Preserving them means protecting not just the corals themselves, but an entire world that depends on their survival. For when these underwater gardens fade, the ocean loses a little of its colour, its shelter and its life.Jumeirah has developed a network of saltwater lagoons which were initially for sea turtle rehabilitation. They transformed into the world's first coral nursery which has become a site for coral restoration in the gulf waters. Even though Dubai seems to be an unlikely place to set this experiment, the observation that some of the corals in the Arabian Gulf have evolved to survive in harsh marine conditions intrigued the scientific community studying climate resilience.The Science of Coral RestorationAl Naseem nursery of Jumeirah, which began as a pilot in 2023, has already produced 2500 coral fragments. Out of these over 300 have been translocated to the sea. The man-made lagoons get water directly from the Arabian Gulf and are connected narrowly to the sea. In order to provide breeding ground, shelter and to hold plankton to the newly bred corals, cave structures have been built inside the lagoons. The project aims to restore corals primarily that were dislocated during construction and those that are at risk due to siltation. Even with sea temperatures rising beyond ideal conditions, scientists believe that the Phoenix effect helped them come to life. Under the Phoenix effect, corals that appear dead regenerate from polyps that survive deep within the skeleton.One of the most interesting aspects of Dubai’s coral restoration effort is how it combines marine conservation with innovative design. The nursery uses a technique called micro-fragmentation, in which healthy coral colonies are divided into tiny pieces. They are then attached to structures which are specially prepared for corals at this stage. Further, under suitable conditions, these fragments can grow and eventually be returned to the sea. This helps in rebuilding damaged reef habitats in natural environments.Beyond Growing CoralsThe maintenance of the coral colonies is much more accessible due to the artificial nature of the structures. Unlike the open-water nurseries, the synthetic conditions with natural light and rich plankton presence have made it possible to maintain the ideal conditions. Fragments of corals are cut and pasted to small concrete structures in the lagoons which are then carefully monitored. As they heal and attach they are transferred to offshore nurseries where they further mature in controlled environments for the next 18 months. The concrete blocks are also made from limestone cement that is sourced locally which makes it a sustainable choice. It provides calcium carbonate which is the element that also forms coral skeletons.However, coral restoration is not simply about growing more corals. Different species create different reef shapes, providing varied habitats for fish and other marine organisms. Their survival must be monitored over time to understand whether restored areas can support a thriving ecosystem. Dubai Reef’s broader programme also aims to create habitats through purpose-built reef modules and advance research into marine conservation.The process is a reminder that restoring nature requires patience. A reef cannot be rebuilt overnight; each fragment needs time to attach, grow and become part of a larger living system.

articles.title: A community in South Australia’s first dark-sky reserve is opposing a proposed hyperscale data centre; residents fear the development could change the rural landscape and threaten the darkness that draws visitors
articles.summary: \"For my part, I know nothing with any certainty, but the sight of the stars makes me dream.\" Vincent van Gogh wrote this in one of his letters to his
articles.body: "For my part, I know nothing with any certainty, but the sight of the stars makes me dream." Vincent van Gogh wrote this in one of his letters to his brother Theo in 1888. More than a century later, the mere sight of stars in a dark sky still reminds us that deep down, we are human. There are very few things left that take us back to ourselves. Art, poetry and stargazing are a few of those. From Aristotle’s Eureka to the Three Wise Men’s hallelujah, the stars have witnessed it all. Today, a community in South Australia is opposing a proposed hyperscale data centre near its dark-sky reserve, fearing that the development could change the rural landscape and threaten the darkness that draws visitors from far and wide.In a world increasingly shaped by technology, even the darkness of the night sky has become something worth protecting. Today, artificial lighting has obscured the view, making exceptionally dark skies increasingly valuable. In South Australia, as reported by ABC (Australian Broadcasting Corporation), residents of Tungkillo are now concerned that a proposed hyperscale data centre and energy hub could threaten the quiet rural landscape and dark skies they cherish. The development, proposed by Melbourne-based Quantum DC, has drawn opposition from locals worried about light and noise pollution. Their concerns have brought a larger question into focus: as digital infrastructure expands, what happens to the natural landscapes and experiences that cannot easily be replaced?Residents fear a data centre could threaten South Australia’s dark skiesOne of the biggest concerns raised by the community is light pollution. Residents fear that the scale of the project could change the character of the surrounding countryside. Light pollution could make it difficult to observe stars and other celestial objects, even in areas far from major cities. Residents also fear that lighting from the facility, along with the noise associated with its operations, could affect the quiet rural environment and the experience that draws stargazers and visitors to the region.Although the proposed site is 5 km away from the River Murray Dark Sky Reserve, residents are concerned about the potential effects on the wider landscape, particularly given the importance of preserving dark skies in an area recognised for its stargazing opportunities.Quantum DC, the company associated with the project, has cited existing energy infrastructure as one of the reasons for selecting this location. The company has also indicated that specialist studies are being undertaken to assess the potential environmental impacts of the project.The development could bring employment opportunities, including jobs during construction and ongoing operational roles. However, for residents, the question remains whether the economic benefits can be balanced with the need to protect their rural landscape and the darkness that makes the region distinctive.The proposal has not yet reached the formal development application stage, meaning its final design and potential impacts remain to be assessed. As the plans progress, the concerns raised by the community are likely to remain central to the debate over how new digital infrastructure should be developed near environmentally and culturally valued landscapes.Why dark-sky reserves matterDark-sky reserves are designated areas intended to protect the natural darkness of the night sky from excessive lighting. In the modern era, major institutions like the World Bank and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), along with prominent academic economists, consider nighttime light (NTL) an indicator of development. However, residents argue that the value of this development must be weighed against the beauty of their night sky. Many people also visit these places to escape the noise and harsh lighting of cities and relax their senses, as these areas offer an opportunity to experience a night sky that is increasingly difficult to see in urban areas, where streetlights, buildings and other sources of illumination obscure the stars.Beyond stargazing, reducing unnecessary artificial light can also benefit nocturnal wildlife, whose feeding, movement and breeding patterns may be affected by excessive illumination. Dark skies can therefore form part of a broader effort to preserve natural environments and protect experiences that depend on them.The River Murray Dark Sky Reserve reflects this value by recognising the importance of preserving dark skies in the region. The debate surrounding the proposed data centre highlights a challenge faced by communities worldwide: how to accommodate expanding infrastructure while maintaining the natural conditions that make certain landscapes unique.As the demand for digital infrastructure continues to grow, the debate around the proposed data centre raises questions about what communities stand to lose in the process. For residents of Tungkillo, protecting the night sky is about preserving more than a view of the stars. It is about safeguarding the character of a landscape that offers a rare connection to the natural world.

articles.title: In 2012 and 2013, Maine removed two old Penobscot River dams to restore migratory routes; by September 2026, the Milford fish lift had counted a preliminary 5.85 million river herring returning upstream
articles.summary: Who knew that a small fish would become the storyteller of one of the biggest wildlife comebacks?
articles.body: Who knew that a small fish would become the storyteller of one of the biggest wildlife comebacks? Imagine a river where millions of fish try to swim upstream every year, only to find concrete barriers blocking access to stretches of water they have travelled for generations. Now imagine what happens when those barriers are removed, and the river's long-blocked routes begin to open up again. Something similar has been unfolding along Maine's Penobscot River in the United States, where a major restoration project has helped migratory fish regain access to parts of the river that were once difficult to reach.In 2012 and 2013, two old dams, the Great Works Dam and the Veazie Dam, were removed as part of the Penobscot River Restoration Project. The effort reopened around 15 kilometres of the river's main channel, while improvements to fish passage at other dams helped fish continue their journey upstream. By October 12, 2026, Maine's Department of Marine Resources had recorded a provisional count of 5,852,487 river herring at the Milford fish lift, offering a striking example of the changes that can follow when a river's natural connections are restored.How removing two dams changed the riverFor decades, dams have played an important role in generating electricity and supporting other human activities, but they can also interrupt the movement of fish between the sea and freshwater habitats where they reproduce. For migratory species, being unable to pass these barriers can mean losing access to important spawning and feeding areas, making it harder for populations to recover.The Penobscot River Restoration Project aimed to address this problem without simply abandoning hydropower altogether. Along with removing the Great Works and Veazie dams, the project included improvements to fish passage at remaining barriers, including a fish lift at Milford Dam, which helps migratory fish move upstream.The changes have been documented in scientific research. A 2023 study published in Marine and Coastal Fisheries, which examined fish communities in the Penobscot River before and after the restoration work, found that the most pronounced changes in fish community composition occurred in sections that had previously been held back by dams. River-dwelling and migratory species became more prevalent in these areas, although the study also noted that different species responded differently to the restoration.Millions of river herring are making the journeyOne of the most interesting parts of this recovery is the return of river herring, which includes alewives and blueback herring, two species that travel from the sea into freshwater rivers to reproduce. For these fish, the journey upstream is an essential part of their life cycle, but dams can make it difficult to reach the waterways they depend on. The difference in the Penobscot River has been striking, with a 2023 study finding that annual river herring counts averaged just 556 fish between 1978 and 2012, when access to the river was still heavily restricted by dams.Following the restoration work, however, the numbers began to rise, crossing 180,000 in 2014 and reaching around 2.3 million by 2018. The recovery has continued since then, with Maine's Department of Marine Resources recording a provisional count of 5,852,487 river herring at the Milford fish lift by October 12, 2026. It is a remarkable change from the earlier counts, showing how reopening migratory routes and improving fish passage can help large numbers of fish return to stretches of a river that were once difficult to reach.Why restoring a river matters beyond fish numbersThe return of migratory fish is important because rivers are not isolated waterways; they are connected ecosystems in which fish movements link freshwater habitats with the sea. Migratory fish can also contribute to food webs, providing food for other animals and helping move nutrients between aquatic environments.However, the recovery of one group of fish does not automatically mean that an entire river ecosystem has returned to its original condition. The Penobscot research found different patterns among different species, and Atlantic salmon and they for instance have continued to occur in comparatively low numbers following the restoration work.Still, the project offers a useful lesson in river conservation: restoring the movement of water and wildlife can make a measurable difference, even in ecosystems that have been shaped by human infrastructure for generations. Sometimes, helping nature recover does not mean building something new, but removing an obstacle that has stood in its way for years.

articles.title: The UK is planning to send giant robotic claws into orbit to grab two dead satellites and drag them into Earth’s atmosphere to burn up, a first-of-its-kind clean-up mission due to launch in 2029, and the public can help name it
articles.summary: The satellite debris in space poses an immense problem in Earth's orbit, which is increasingly crowded, especially with defunct satellites that continue
articles.body: The satellite debris in space poses an immense problem in Earth's orbit, which is increasingly crowded, especially with defunct satellites that continue to circle the planet. According to Smithsonian magazine, the United Kingdom is preparing a mission to declutter Earth's orbit. It is preparing to tackle part of the growing problem of satellites debris with an unusual spacecraft featuring giant robotic claws. The spacecraft is designed to capture two defunct satellites and bring them down into the atmosphere to incinerate them. This is a first-of-its-kind clean-up mission due to launch in 2029, and the public can help name it.Rob Atchison, Managing Director of ClearSpace UK in a statement dated 15th October 2026 shared, “Our next step is to design, build and test a spacecraft that can get close, safely, to an object never designed to be caught, and take control of it. We will do this with partners across the UK supply chain, working towards launch in 2029.” The mission, known as the UK Active Debris Removal (UK ADR) programme, is developed with the UK Space Agency and ClearSpace UK. The project will demonstrate how specially designed robotic equipment can remove objects from orbit rather than leave them there indefinitely. Furthermore, the spacecraft is expected to complete its mission by 2032, marking a significant step toward making space operations more sustainable.How the robotic claws will capture dead satellitesUnlike a conventional spacecraft designed to carry equipment or people, the proposed vehicle will have to approach objects that were never built to be captured. Its robotic claws are intended to grip satellites that may be moving or tumbling through space, making the operation considerably more complicated than simply reaching out and grabbing an object.The spacecraft will need to match the movement of its targets before attempting to capture them. This requires carefully controlled manoeuvres and precise navigation to bring the vehicle close enough to the satellites without causing an additional collision. Once secured, the spacecraft will guide them toward a lower orbit, allowing Earth's atmosphere to slow them down and generate the heat that causes them to disintegrate during re-entry.The technology is being developed by ClearSpace UK, the British branch of an in-orbit services company specialising in spacecraft operations. The mission will use a refuelable spacecraft designed with the possibility of future use in mind, potentially opening the door to vehicles that can undertake further work in orbit instead of being discarded after a single operation.Why removing space junk mattersSatellites have become an important part of everyday life, supporting services that people often take for granted. GPS navigation, weather forecasting, communications and several other systems rely on equipment operating above Earth. When satellites stop functioning, however, they can remain in orbit and become potential hazards for other spacecraft.The problem extends beyond old satellites. Defunct rocket stages and fragments left behind by previous space activities also contribute to orbital debris where even relatively smaller pieces can pose a threat because objects in orbit travel at extraordinary speeds. According to the official orbital radar data, there are nearly 32,000 tracked objects. Smithsonian Magazine in its report on the same states that roughly half of these objects are space debris. With so much junk present in the orbit, a collision can damage an operational satellite and produce additional fragments, creating further risks for other objects sharing the same region of space.As more satellites are launched to meet the growing demand for communications and other services, managing the debris already in orbit becomes incredibly crucial. However, one mission alone cannot clear the entire orbital environment of waste and junk that has perhaps been present for years now. But, The UK ADR programme aims to illustrate that a single spacecraft can remove more than one satellite during an operation, an approach that could help make future debris-removal missions more practical.A mission the public can help nameAlongside the technical work, the UK Space Agency has launched a public competition for its trash disposal mission, inviting people to suggest a name for the spacecraft. The initiative offers the public an opportunity to contribute to the country's first nationally commissioned active debris-removal mission.Entries for the UK Space Agency competition are open until December 10, 2026. According to the agency, the selected name will be displayed on the spacecraft, giving the winning suggestion a place in the history of the project. The naming competition also offers a way to bring attention to an issue that can otherwise seem distant from everyday concerns. Although space debris may appear far removed from life on the ground, the satellites affected by it support technologies used by millions of people. Keeping their orbital environment safe is therefore closely connected to maintaining the services people depend on.As Dr Alice Bunn, Co-Director of the UK Space Agency in a statement has noted, "This mission is about much more than removing debris. It is about developing the capabilities that will enable future servicing, assembly and manufacturing in orbit.” Future spacecraft may be designed not only to remove unwanted objects but also to inspect, repair or refuel satellites that are still useful. Such capabilities could reduce the need to replace expensive equipment and help make long-term space activity more sustainable.
